---
title: "Gaussianization: Learn the Density, Then Measure"
---



Road 2 keeps hitting the same wall.  The
[mutual information page](03-mutual-information.qmd) estimated $p(x,y)$ with
a crude histogram; the [windows page](04-windows-and-blocks.qmd) fell back on
Gaussian closed forms and admitted they were *lower bounds*.  Both are
versions of one compromise: **assume** the density's shape.  This page takes
the other branch of the fork — **learn** the shape — and in doing so closes
the ladder.

The trick sounds too simple to work: *transform the data until it is
Gaussian, and keep the receipts.*

---

## It All Comes Back to $p(\mathbf{x})$

Before the trick, the wall it climbs.  Every Road-2 measure — entropy, mutual
information, total correlation — is the *same integral* against the density,
and helpless without it:

$$H(\mathbf{x}) = -\!\int p(\mathbf{x})\log p(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x},
\quad
I(X;Y) = \!\int p(\mathbf{x})\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(x)\,p(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x},
\quad
T(\mathbf{x}) = \!\int p(\mathbf{x})\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{\prod_i p(x_i)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}.$$

Road 1 dodged this entirely — distances and kernels never write down a
density.  Road 2 cannot: **the whole game is estimating $p(\mathbf{x})$.**  So
the real question is how hard that estimation is, and the answer depends
brutally on dimension.

### One dimension — easy

In 1-D you have three options and all of them work.  Bin the data into a
**histogram**; *assume* a shape and fit a **parametric Gaussian**; or *learn*
the shape with a **kernel density estimate**.  The only thing that separates
them is honesty about shape — a Gaussian nails a bell and botches a skew, while
the learned curve tracks whatever the data does:

::: {#cell-fig-density-1d .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng_1d = np.random.default_rng(3)
easy = rng_1d.normal(0, 1, 1500)                         # a clean bell
hard = skewnorm.rvs(6, size=1500, random_state=7)        # skewed, heavy on one side

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3))
for ax, data, name in [(axes[0], easy, "easy — a bell"),
                       (axes[1], hard, "hard — skewed")]:
    g = np.linspace(data.min() - 0.5, data.max() + 0.5, 300)
    ax.hist(data, bins=32, density=True, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95,
            edgecolor="white", lw=0.6, label="histogram (data)")
    ax.plot(g, norm.pdf(g, data.mean(), data.std()), color=CRASH, lw=2.4,
            ls="--", label="assume: Gaussian")
    ax.plot(g, gaussian_kde(data)(g), color=COOL, lw=2.6, label="learn: KDE")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On a skewed return (right) the Gaussian — pinned to mean and variance — leans the wrong way, while the KDE follows the data. Histogram in grey, assumed Gaussian dashed, learned KDE solid.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-density-1d-output-1.png){#fig-density-1d width=1184 height=380}

### Two dimensions — still manageable

Stack the two and you can still see the whole density: a scatter with its two
marginals, an assumed Gaussian contour, a learned KDE contour.  A Gaussian's
*only* dependence is correlation — its contour is always an ellipse, the shadow
of its covariance — so it tilts toward the banks' blob but sits blind over the
V.  The learned density wraps the bend:

::: {#cell-fig-density-2d .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
a2, b2, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=900)
u2, v2 = datasets.convex_payoff(n=900)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
for ax, x, y, col, name in [(axes[0], a2, b2, COOL, "easy — a tilted blob"),
                            (axes[1], u2, v2, WARM, "hard — a V")]:
    X = np.column_stack([x, y])
    g = np.linspace(X.min() - 0.5, X.max() + 0.5, 130)
    GXg, GYg = np.meshgrid(g, g)
    Zg = multivariate_normal(X.mean(0), np.cov(X.T)).pdf(np.dstack([GXg, GYg]))   # assume
    Zk = gaussian_kde(X.T)(np.vstack([GXg.ravel(), GYg.ravel()])).reshape(GXg.shape)  # learn
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, c=col, alpha=0.32, edgecolors="none")
    ax.contour(GXg, GYg, Zg, levels=5, colors=[CRASH], linewidths=1.1, linestyles="dashed")
    ax.contour(GXg, GYg, Zk, levels=5, colors=[INK], linewidths=1.1)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

On the tilted blob (left) both fit; on the V (right) the Gaussian misses the bend while the KDE wraps it.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-density-2d-output-1.png){#fig-density-2d width=1184 height=416}

### Many dimensions — you go blind

Past three dimensions the picture is gone and the histogram dies with it.  A
grid of bins needs roughly $10^{d}$ samples to fill — the **curse of
dimensionality** — so by a handful of assets a histogram of daily returns would
ask for more days than the universe has had.  There is no plot to draw and no
table to count:

::: {#cell-fig-density-manyd .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng_md = np.random.default_rng(3)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.6, 2.7))
d1 = rng_md.normal(0, 1, 1200)                                  # 1-D: a histogram
g1 = np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 200)
axes[0].hist(d1, bins=28, density=True, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95,
             edgecolor="white", lw=0.5)
axes[0].plot(g1, gaussian_kde(d1)(g1), color=COOL, lw=2.4)
axes[0].set_title("1-D · a histogram", fontsize=11)
p2 = rng_md.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, 0.6], [0.6, 1]], 500)  # 2-D: a density
gg = np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 90); GX2, GY2 = np.meshgrid(gg, gg)
Zk2 = gaussian_kde(p2.T)(np.vstack([GX2.ravel(), GY2.ravel()])).reshape(GX2.shape)
axes[1].scatter(p2[:, 0], p2[:, 1], s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
axes[1].contour(GX2, GY2, Zk2, levels=5, colors=[INK], linewidths=1.0)
axes[1].set_title("2-D · a density", fontsize=11)
q = rng_md.normal(0, 1, (200, 2))                              # d-D: no picture
axes[2].scatter(q[:, 0], q[:, 1], s=8, c=GRID, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none")
axes[2].text(0.5, 0.5, "?", transform=axes[2].transAxes, ha="center", va="center",
             fontsize=60, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
axes[2].set_title("d-D · no picture", fontsize=11, color=CRASH)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor(GRID)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

The only survivor is to LEARN an invertible density.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-density-manyd-output-1.png){#fig-density-manyd width=1136 height=308}

### Assume it, or learn it

Two families answer the estimation question, and the fork between them is the
fork this whole page is about.

**Assume a family — *parametric*.**  Pick a shape (Gaussian, Student-$t$,
mixture) and fit a few numbers.  Cheap, frugal with data, scales to high
dimension — but **rigid**: a Gaussian's only dependence is correlation, so any
bend or fat tail is structurally invisible to it, no matter how many samples
you feed it.

**Learn the shape — *nonparametric*.**  Let the data carve the density: a KDE
in low dimension, and in high dimension an **invertible learned map**.  Flexible
enough for Vs, fat tails, and modes — at the cost of more data and more compute.

Gaussianization is how we get the second one in high dimension without a
histogram: **learn an invertible map that turns the data into a Gaussian** —
flexible shape on the way in, exact likelihoods on the way out.  That map is the
trick this page promised, and the next section is its mechanism.

---

## Rung 8 · The Iteration

Reshaping each marginal to a bell curve is easy (a rank map does it exactly).
But dependence lives *between* the axes, beyond any per-axis map — reshape
both marginals of a V and the V survives.  The fix: **rotate** the axes, so
leftover dependence resurfaces as non-Gaussian marginals, which the 1-D move
can flatten.  Alternate the two and the structure has nowhere left to hide:

::: {#cell-fig-gaussianization-iterate .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
u_g, v_g = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1200, seed=0)
XG = np.column_stack([u_g, v_g])              # (n_days, 2)
XG = (XG - XG.mean(0)) / XG.std(0)            # standardize each column


def gauss_marginals(D: Float[Array, "n_days 2"]) -> Float[Array, "n_days 2"]:
    """The 1-D move, applied per axis: each marginal → exactly 𝒩(0, 1)."""
    return np.column_stack([gaussianize_1d(D[:, 0]), gaussianize_1d(D[:, 1])])


def rotate(D: Float[Array, "n_days 2"], deg: float) -> Float[Array, "n_days 2"]:
    """Rotate the cloud by θ: x ↦ R(θ)·x, with R = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]."""
    θ = np.deg2rad(deg)
    R_θ = np.array([[np.cos(θ), -np.sin(θ)],
                    [np.sin(θ),  np.cos(θ)]])        # (2, 2) rotation matrix
    return einx.dot("n d, k d -> n k", D, R_θ)       # apply R to every day's pair


rng_g = np.random.default_rng(0)
P2 = gauss_marginals(XG)                      # reshape marginals — V survives
P3 = gauss_marginals(rotate(P2, 45))          # rotate, reshape — V starts to melt
P4 = P3
for _ in range(25):                           # …repeat until round
    P4 = gauss_marginals(rotate(P4, rng_g.uniform(20, 70)))
# I(X;Y) before and after, in bits (helper returns nats → ÷ ln 2)
mi0 = mutual_information_xy(XG[:, 0], XG[:, 1]) / np.log(2)
mi1 = mutual_information_xy(P4[:, 0], P4[:, 1]) / np.log(2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12.5, 3.5))
for ax, (ttl, Dk) in zip(axes, [(f"the data — a V\nMI = {mi0:.2f} bits", XG),
                                ("reshape marginals\n(still a V)", P2),
                                ("rotate, reshape again", P3),
                                (f"…repeat → a Gaussian ball\nMI = {mi1:.2f} bits", P4)]):
    ax.scatter(Dk[:, 0], Dk[:, 1], s=6, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Gaussianization, step by step. Panel 1: the convex pair, carrying over a bit of mutual information. Panel 2: reshaping each marginal to a perfect Gaussian leaves the V — and the MI — untouched. Panel 3: rotate 45° and reshape again; the structure starts to dissolve. Panel 4: a few dozen rotate-reshape rounds later the joint is a round Gaussian ball and the mutual information is gone. What the loop had to remove IS the dependence.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-gaussianization-iterate-output-1.png){#fig-gaussianization-iterate width=1484 height=416}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
The loop above is the real mechanism, written in four lines: the 1-D
rank-to-Gaussian map (`lectures.gaussianization.gaussianize_1d`) alternated
with rotations.  The production RBIG (the `rbig` package) chooses rotations
more cleverly, tracks the exact change-of-variables Jacobian, and thereby
yields exact log-likelihoods and MI estimates — see the
[Gaussianization chapter](../gaussianization/index.qmd) for the full machine.
:::

### Why This Measures Anything

Because every step is **invertible**, the procedure is bookkeeping, not
destruction.  The bits of mutual information that vanish between panel 1 and
panel 4 did not disappear — they were *paid out* by the transform, and the
change-of-variables formula records the price exactly.  **The dependence the
loop must remove is the data's total correlation.**  That turns a generative
trick into an estimator: run the loop, sum the receipts, read off
$T(\mathbf{x})$ in bits — in any dimension, with no histogram in sight.

### The Idea Underneath

A Gaussian is the *least-committal* distribution consistent with a given
covariance — it assumes nothing beyond the correlations measured.  So whatever
Gaussianization must *work* to remove is exactly the structure that correlation
never implied: the nonlinear, tail-driven dependence.

This is the first appearance of the principle the whole course turns on:
**claim only what your evidence justifies.**  The same invertible machine —
re-implemented in JAX as `gauss_flows` — runs *backward* in Lecture 3 to
generate scenarios and propagate risk.

---

## Fit the V Three Ways

Words are cheap; let the V judge.  Here are the three density estimators of the
fork — an *assumed* Gaussian, an *assumed* Student-$t$ (the heaviest-tailed
ellipse), and a *learned* RBIG — fit to the same convex pair, each scored two
ways.  The **log-likelihood** asks how well the model explains the data it saw;
the **recovered mutual information** asks how much dependence the model's own
samples carry.

A note on the second score, because it is the one pitfall here.  RBIG's
built-in MI routine is tuned for asymmetric dependence and reads the symmetric
V as nearly independent — the wrong answer.  The honest move is to ask each
fitted model what it *believes*: draw samples from it, then histogram-estimate
the MI of those samples.  A model that captures the V will reproduce it when
sampled, and that MI is what it has actually learned.

::: {#cell-fig-fit-v-three-ways .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import rbig

u8, v8 = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1200, seed=0)
X8 = np.column_stack([u8, v8]).astype(float)              # (n_days, 2)
loc8, cov8 = X8.mean(0), np.cov(X8.T)                     # sample mean & covariance

# --- assume: a Gaussian (its only dependence is correlation) ---
gN = multivariate_normal(loc8, cov8)

# --- assume: a Student-t; pick df by max mean log-lik, shape = cov·(df−2)/df ---
#     so the model covariance matches the sample covariance
dfg = max(((d, multivariate_t(loc8, cov8 * (d - 2) / d, df=d).logpdf(X8).mean())
           for d in (3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15)), key=lambda z: z[1])[0]
tN = multivariate_t(loc8, cov8 * (dfg - 2) / dfg, df=dfg)

# --- learn: RBIG (the production iterative Gaussianizer) ---
mR = rbig.AnnealedRBIG(random_state=0); mR.fit(X8)


def mi_bits(s: Float[Array, "n 2"]) -> float:
    """Histogram-MI of a 2-column sample, in bits (helper is nats → ÷ ln 2)."""
    return mutual_information_xy(s[:, 0], s[:, 1]) / np.log(2)


# each model's recovered MI = MI of its OWN samples (RBIG's MI routine misreads the V)
gsamp = gN.rvs(7000, random_state=1)
tsamp = tN.rvs(7000, random_state=1)
rsamp = np.asarray(mR.sample(7000, random_state=1))
mis = [mi_bits(gsamp), mi_bits(tsamp), mi_bits(rsamp)]
trueMI = mi_bits(X8)                                      # data's own histogram MI

# mean log-likelihood per point (RBIG via change-of-variables)
gll = gN.logpdf(X8).mean()
tll = tN.logpdf(X8).mean()
rll = -rbig.negative_log_likelihood(mR, X8)

# density grids for the contours (RBIG via a KDE of its samples)
gx = np.linspace(X8[:, 0].min() - 1, X8[:, 0].max() + 1, 110)
gy = np.linspace(X8[:, 1].min() - 1, X8[:, 1].max() + 1, 110)
GXc, GYc = np.meshgrid(gx, gy)
Zg = gN.pdf(np.dstack([GXc, GYc]))
Zt = tN.pdf(np.dstack([GXc, GYc]))
Zr = gaussian_kde(rsamp[:2500].T)(np.vstack([GXc.ravel(), GYc.ravel()])).reshape(GXc.shape)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.2))
gsp = GridSpec(2, 3, width_ratios=[4, 1.1, 2.5], height_ratios=[1, 4],
               wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
axT = fig.add_subplot(gsp[0, 0])          # top marginal
axMn = fig.add_subplot(gsp[1, 0])         # joint scatter + contours
axRt = fig.add_subplot(gsp[1, 1])         # right marginal
axSt = fig.add_subplot(gsp[:, 2]); axSt.axis("off")   # scorecard panel

axMn.scatter(X8[:, 0], X8[:, 1], s=7, c=GRID, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axMn.contour(GXc, GYc, Zg, levels=5, colors=[CRASH], linewidths=1.2, linestyles="dashed")
axMn.contour(GXc, GYc, Zt, levels=5, colors=[WARM], linewidths=1.1, linestyles="dotted")
axMn.contour(GXc, GYc, Zr, levels=5, colors=[COOL], linewidths=1.5)
axMn.set_xticks([]); axMn.set_yticks([]); despine(axMn)
axMn.legend(handles=[Line2D([0], [0], color=COOL, lw=1.6, label="RBIG (learned)"),
                     Line2D([0], [0], color=WARM, lw=1.1, ls=":", label="Student-t"),
                     Line2D([0], [0], color=CRASH, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="Gaussian")],
            fontsize=9.5, frameon=False, loc="upper center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.03))
axT.hist(X8[:, 0], bins=40, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", lw=0.4)
axT.axis("off")
axRt.hist(X8[:, 1], bins=40, orientation="horizontal", color="#c9cdd4",
          alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", lw=0.4)
axRt.axis("off")
axSt.text(0.0, 0.97, f"n = {len(X8)} samples", fontsize=11, color="#666",
          transform=axSt.transAxes)
for j, (nm, c, ll, mi) in enumerate([("RBIG (learned)", COOL, rll, mis[2]),
                                     ("Student-t", WARM, tll, mis[1]),
                                     ("Gaussian", CRASH, gll, mis[0])]):
    yb = 0.82 - j * 0.27
    axSt.text(0.0, yb, nm, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color=c, transform=axSt.transAxes)
    axSt.text(0.06, yb - 0.085, f"log-lik  {ll:+.2f}", fontsize=11, color=INK,
              transform=axSt.transAxes)
    axSt.text(0.06, yb - 0.165, f"MI  {mi:.2f} bits", fontsize=11, color=INK,
              transform=axSt.transAxes)
axSt.text(0.0, 0.02, f"true MI = {trueMI:.2f} bits", fontsize=11, style="italic",
          color=INK, transform=axSt.transAxes)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Side panel: each model's mean log-likelihood and its recovered MI in bits, against the data's true histogram MI. Both ellipses sit blind over the bend; only the RBIG contour wraps the V — and only RBIG's likelihood and recovered bits come close to the truth.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-fit-v-three-ways-output-1.png){#fig-fit-v-three-ways width=1047 height=414}

The two ellipses are interchangeable here — the Student-$t$ buys fatter tails

The lesson is sharp.  An assumed shape is cheap and scales, but it can only
report the dependence its *form* allows — and an ellipse's form is correlation.
The learned map pays in compute and earns the rest: the likelihood the others
leave on the table *and* the bits of dependence the bend actually carries.

---

## Synthesis — The Two Roads, Grown

Look back at the ladder.  Every tool was one of two roads:

**Road 1 — no density needed:**
```
measure = compare( transform(x) , transform(y) )
```
Pearson, Spearman, distance correlation, and HSIC/CKA all fit this template.
They differ only in the transform and the distance/kernel used.

**Road 2 — through the density:**
```
measure = D_KL( p(x,y) || p(x)·p(y) )
```
Mutual information, total correlation.  The density must come from somewhere:
*assume* its shape (parametric — cheap, wrong in tails) or *learn* it
(generative — Gaussianization, flows).

The *transform* is the thread: a fixed, hand-picked map on Road 1; a learned,
invertible map on the generative branch of Road 2.  An invertible transform
that simplifies the data hands you the density for free.

**The axis that actually orders the ladder is complexity, not detection.**  By
now almost every rung past Pearson *detects* the V — distance correlation, CKA,
and the learned MI all catch the bend.  What separates the tools is what they
cost and what they hand back.  Road 1 is a single branching path of *scores*,
each rung buying reach with compute: Pearson → Spearman → dCor → CKA.  Road 2 is
a path of *densities*, and it splits once more — *assume* the shape (Gaussian,
Student-$t$ — cheap, rigid) before you *learn* it (RBIG — costly, exact).  Read
the picture left to right as rising complexity:

::: {#cell-fig-two-roads .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.6))
ax.set_xlim(0, 11); ax.set_ylim(0, 6.6); ax.axis("off")


def _station(x, y, label, color, hi=False):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - 0.78, y - 0.32), 1.56, 0.64,
                                boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.14",
                                fc="white", ec=color, lw=2.8 if hi else 1.8, zorder=3))
```

Detection is the easy part — most rungs past Pearson catch the V.  The real
trade-off is **complexity**: a score is cheap and one-shot; the full density
costs more and is data-hungry, but it is the only branch that is *invertible* —
and so the only branch that lets you **sample, propagate, and price the tails**,
not merely detect them.

## Every Method, Both Characters

The whole ladder on one chart, and both characters scored down it: the four
Road-1 rungs (Pearson, Spearman, distance correlation, CKA), then mutual
information read through each of the three densities (Gaussian, Student-$t$,
RBIG).  To put the bits on the same $[0,1]$ axis as the correlations, each MI is
mapped to its **Linfoot $R = \sqrt{1 - e^{-2I}}$** — the rescaling that returns
exactly $|\rho|$ for a Gaussian pair, so a parametric MI and a correlation sit
naturally side by side.

::: {#cell-fig-every-method .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import rbig


def char_scores(x: Float[Array, "n_days"], y: Float[Array, "n_days"]) -> list[float]:
    """The full ladder for one pair, every entry on [0, 1]."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    X = np.column_stack([x, y])
    loc, cov = X.mean(0), np.cov(X.T)
    g = multivariate_normal(loc, cov)
    df = max(((d, multivariate_t(loc, cov * (d - 2) / d, df=d).logpdf(X).mean())
              for d in (3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15)), key=lambda z: z[1])[0]
    t = multivariate_t(loc, cov * (df - 2) / df, df=df)
    m = rbig.AnnealedRBIG(random_state=0); m.fit(X)

    def mi_R(s: Float[Array, "n 2"]) -> float:
        # MI of the model's OWN samples (nats), mapped to Linfoot R ∈ [0, 1]
        return linfoot_r(mutual_information_xy(s[:, 0], s[:, 1]))

    return [abs(pearsonr(x, y)[0]), abs(spearmanr(x, y)[0]),
            distance_correlation(x, y), cka_rbf(x, y),
            mi_R(g.rvs(8000, random_state=1)),
            mi_R(t.rvs(8000, random_state=1)),
            mi_R(np.asarray(m.sample(8000, random_state=1)))]


a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=1000)
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1000)
banks, convex = char_scores(a, b), char_scores(u, v)
methods = ["Pearson", "Spearman", "dist\ncorr", "CKA",
           "MI·\nGauss", "MI·\nt", "MI·\nRBIG"]
xs = np.arange(7); wbar = 0.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.5, 4.5))
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 1.5, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)        # the linear-only rungs
ax.axvline(3.5, color=GRID, lw=1.6, ls="--")          # Road 1 | Road 2 divide
ax.bar(xs - wbar / 2, banks, wbar, color=COOL, label="Banks (a line)")
ax.bar(xs + wbar / 2, convex, wbar, color=WARM, label="Convex (a V)")
ax.text(1.5, 1.0, "Road 1 · a score", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(5.0, 1.0, "Road 2 · MI via a density", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(0.5, 0.14, "linear:\nblind to the V", ha="center", fontsize=10.5,
        color=CRASH, style="italic", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(methods, fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("dependence detected  (0–1)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.1)
ax.legend(fontsize=12, frameon=False, ncol=2, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.03))
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On the V, the linear rungs AND the parametric MIs (Gaussian, t) stay flat — only distance corr, CKA, and MI·RBIG catch the bend.](05-gaussianization_files/figure-html/fig-every-method-output-1.png){#fig-every-method width=1364 height=526}
:::
:::


**Opposite blind spots, made concrete.**  On the **Banks** every column is tall:
a near-Gaussian line is exactly what correlation, ranks, kernels, *and* a fitted
Gaussian all see, so they agree.  On the **V** the chart splits cleanly — the
linear rungs (Pearson, Spearman) *and* the parametric MIs (Gaussian, Student-$t$)
all collapse, because each is, at heart, an ellipse; only **distance corr, CKA,
and MI·RBIG** rise to meet the bend.  No single number is the whole truth, and
the chart shows exactly which numbers fail and why: anything that can only draw
an ellipse is blind to a V.

## The Punchline — For the Lab

With the ladder in hand, the hands-on labs point these tools at real S&P 500
returns.  The running characters return as their real selves (JPMorgan, Bank of
America, ...).  You will find that two banks share roughly **0.7 bits** of
information and fall into their worst days together roughly **7× more often**
than independence allows — the dependence that correlation cannot see, and the
one that actually threatens a portfolio.
